evidence_quotes.quote: Nesse sentido, são objetivos do presente artigo identificar aspectos atuais da situação de acesso a água para consumo humano, bem como enriquecer o debate sobre os desafios para o atendimento das necessidades humanas por água na Amazônia Brasileira, considerando em distintas escalas espaciais, aspectos de infraestrutura e a necessidade de se compreender dinâmicas socioculturais.

Em um panorama regional verificamos um sério déficit para a Amazônia Legal, sendo que o percentual de domicílios permanentes ligados à rede de abastecimento de água na região em 2009 foi de 58,5%, bastante inferior ao nacional no mesmo ano (83,1%). De modo mais alarmante consta o percentual de domicílios em estados amazônicos com ligação à rede de esgotos sanitários, que em 2009 foi de apenas 9,4%, enquanto o nacional figurou 52,5%.

Considerando que o crescimento econômico deveria acarretar em melhores condições de vida para a população, apresentamos na Tabela 1 uma possibilidade de análise integrada entre crescimento de PIB per capita e de acesso a serviços de água e esgotos entre 2002 e 2009.

Este estudo tem como objetivo explorar condicionantes de acesso à água para consumo humano, considerando aspectos ambientais, socioculturais e de infraestrutura. Para isso, analisam-se: a precária cobertura por saneamento básico na região, por meio de macroindicadores; e estudos de caso em distintas escalas espaciais
Não havia cobrança proporcional à vazão de água utilizada por domicílio, simplesmente cobrava-se valor fixo mensal de R$ 9,00 por ligação, fato que incidia grandes desperdícios de água aduzida;

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water and sanitation/sewage service access across the nine states of the Brazilian Legal Amazon and in four local case-study settings in Amazonas State (Iauaretê, São Gabriel da Cachoeira, Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve, and Manaus).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (both plain_criterion2_decision and active decision are exclude). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the article does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor as a determinant of service access: its stated and analysed determinants are macroeconomic growth (state GDP per capita), environmental and hydrological conditions (surface-water abundance, seasonal flood cycles, landfill aquifer contamination), physical infrastructure deficits, and sociocultural practices, mythical beliefs, taboos, and risk perceptions. Passing descriptive remarks—such as municipal managers' perceptions of deforestation vs. water pollution (IBGE 2008), a literature reference to political 'estratégia da escassez' (Rebouças 2004), a flat R$ 9.00/month fee causing water waste in São Gabriel da Cachoeira, private concessionaire Águas do Amazonas's diagnostic report in Manaus, Portaria 518/2004 water-quality thresholds, and general closing reflections on charging in non-monetized communities—are unanalysed background context rather than studied exposures. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules governing connection/affordability/disconnection, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access) is empirically analysed.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains a descriptive secondary-data comparison of state-level IBGE indicators (PNAD 2002-2009 household water and sewage network coverage vs. 2002-2009 GDP per capita in Table 1 and Graph 1), alongside non-systematic narrative summaries of four previously published empirical field studies conducted by the authors and colleagues in Amazonas.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports relevant service-access outcomes, including the percentage of permanent private households connected to public water supply and sewage networks by state (2002-2009), counts of residents with precarious or no public water access in Manaus, and household reliance on alternative sources (wells, rainwater, river/stream water, and public taps).
criterion_notes.c5: While state-level populations, macroeconomic exposure (GDP per capita), and network-connection outcomes are identifiable in the secondary IBGE comparison, the paper has no dedicated methodology section, narratively summarizes separate prior case studies without a systematic synthesis protocol, and has no identifiable legal or administrative exposure.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Portuguese, which is directly eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Descriptive ecological comparison of secondary state-level macro-indicators (IBGE PNAD and GDP data, 2002-2009) combined with a non-systematic narrative overview of four previously published local case studies
population_and_sample: 9 states of the Brazilian Legal Amazon (25,474,365 inhabitants in 2010; permanent private households in IBGE PNAD 2002-2009) and four summarized case-study settings in Amazonas State: Iauaretê (~2,700 inhabitants; 65 water samples), São Gabriel da Cachoeira (~39,129 municipal / ~18,000 urban inhabitants), four Mamirauá riverine communities (~350 inhabitants), and Manaus (~1,802,014 inhabitants, including prior surveys of 296 households in Santa Etelvina and 162 households in Novo Israel)
exposure: Macroeconomic growth (state GDP per capita, 2002-2009), environmental/hydrological factors (water abundance, seasonal flooding, landfill aquifer contamination), physical infrastructure deficits, and sociocultural beliefs, water-source preferences, and risk perceptions (no legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism analysed)
outcome: Percentage of permanent private households connected to public water supply and sewage networks (2002-2009), unserved or precariously served population counts, household drinking-water source utilization (wells, rainwater, river water, public taps), water contamination, and intestinal parasite prevalence
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper examines household drinking-water and sewage access in the Brazilian Legal Amazon using secondary IBGE state macro-indicators (2002-2009) and narrative summaries of four previously published case studies in Amazonas, its analysed determinants are macroeconomic growth (GDP per capita), environmental/hydrological conditions, physical infrastructure deficits, and sociocultural practices, beliefs, and perceptions. It does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or rule-type governance mechanism governing water or sanitation service access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2.
